questions.prompt: What is the difference between API and ABI compatibility?
options: ABI compatibility implies that the source never needs any change at all, ever
API: source still compiles. ABI: a compiled program still runs with the new binary
API concerns the headers only, while ABI concerns only the documentation files
They are two names for the same thing, so keeping one always keeps the other
questions.explanation: ABI covers symbol names, calling conventions, type sizes and layouts, and vtables; it matters when binaries are swapped without recompiling.

questions.prompt: Which change to a public struct that is passed by pointer across a shared-library boundary is ABI-breaking?
options: Inserting a new field between two existing fields
Adding a comment above one of the fields
Adding a new free function to the same header
Renaming a parameter of a function in the header
questions.explanation: Old binaries use the old offsets, so they read the wrong fields and may overflow their object.

questions.prompt: An extern "C" library function throws a C++ exception and the caller is Python via ctypes. What happens?
options: Python converts it into a Python exception that ctypes raises to the caller
The process terminates (undefined behavior): exceptions must not cross the C boundary
The exception is ignored and execution simply continues after the call
The C runtime catches it and returns -1 to the Python caller
questions.explanation: The caller cannot unwind C++ frames; catch everything at the boundary and return an error code.

questions.prompt: A public struct has 3 doubles and an int, laid out with natural alignment on x86-64 (no reordering). What is sizeof the struct in bytes? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: 3 x 8 = 24 bytes, then the 4-byte int at offset 24, padded to a multiple of the struct alignment (8): 32 bytes.

questions.prompt: Frame* grab(); appears in a C++ header with no comment. What does the signature leave unspecified?
options: Who owns and frees the returned frame and how long it stays valid
The name of the function and its namespace
Nothing is left open; raw pointers always mean a borrowed object
The return type of the function and whether it is a pointer
questions.explanation: A raw pointer return can mean new object (caller frees), internal buffer (valid until next call) or shared resource. The contract must be written or encoded in a type.

questions.prompt: A library exports these functions: c_add (extern "C"), cxx_add(int,int), robot::cxx_add2(int,int), takes_vector(const std::vector<int>&). How many of them can be called from Python ctypes by their plain source name? Give an integer.
questions.explanation: Only the extern "C" function keeps its plain symbol name; the other three are mangled.

questions.prompt: Describe the two-layer design for exposing a C++ robot-arm library to users built with different compilers: what is in the binary interface, what is in the wrapper, and who owns what.
rubric: Binary interface: extern "C" functions, opaque handle with create/destroy, error codes, no exceptions or standard types.
Header-only C++ wrapper: RAII (unique_ptr with deleter), move-only, translates codes to exceptions.
Ownership: the creator/wrapper owns the handle; destroy releases it exactly once; documented thread and lifetime rules.
questions.explanation: Rubric-guided: compare your answer with each rubric point; this question is not automatically graded.
